sections.h2: What does the Pike County Recorder of Deeds do?
sections.html:
The office records and indexes real estate documents for Pike County, such as deeds, mortgages and mortgage satisfactions. It also acts as a collection agent for the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, which is why realty transfer tax is paid at the same counter as the recording fee.

The county's Recorder of Deeds page lists the office at 506 Broad Street in Milford, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 to 4:30, with a phone line at 570-296-3508. Checks go to "Pike County Recorder of Deeds." A returned document carries a $10 return fee.

Recording comes last in a sale and decides whether the buyer's name shows up in the public index. A deed that sits in a drawer, or one that is rejected, leaves the seller on record as the owner. That matters for property tax bills, liability and any lien searches that follow.

sections.h2: How do I record a deed in Pike County?
sections.html:
You can deliver the deed to the Milford office or send it through an electronic recording vendor. The county names two vendors on its recorder page, and both handle title companies and law offices every day.

  • Simplifile: 800-460-5657, erecord@simplifile.com
  • CSC: 866-652-0111, erecording@cscglobal.com
  • In person or by mail: 506 Broad Street, Milford, PA 18337, with one check for the fee and a separate amount for transfer tax if the deed carries one

The county's published fee schedule changes from time to time, so ask the office for the current deed fee before you write a check. A check in the wrong amount is one of the reasons a package comes back.

When a title company or attorney closes your sale, they normally prepare the deed, calculate the tax and file it. Ask them for the recording confirmation or the book and page reference after closing, and keep it with your sale papers.

sections.h2: Why do Pike County deeds get returned?
sections.html:
The recorder publishes a short checklist of defects. Most of them are clerical, and every one can be fixed before the deed leaves your hands.

  • The acknowledgment date falls before the date on the caption.
  • The acknowledgment leaves out the county, state, date, the names and titles of the people appearing, or the notary's signature, seal and expiration date. The office treats that acknowledgment as defective.
  • The deed does not name the township, county and state where the property sits.
  • The amount written in words differs from the amount in numbers.
  • A document that refers to an earlier mortgage does not give that mortgage's book and page.
  • A set of papers for one transaction is not numbered in the order they should be recorded.
  • Property crossing two municipalities does not show the split of local transfer tax in dollars.
  • The deed lacks the grantee's address, or the grantee address is unsigned.
  • A foreign language document arrives without a written English translation.

If you are selling by yourself without a closing attorney, read this list against your deed line by line. The re-recording costs from a wrong document order fall on whoever submitted it.

sections.h2: How much transfer tax applies to a Pike County sale?
sections.html:
Pennsylvania charges a state realty transfer tax of 1 percent of the value of the property transferred. The Department of Revenue says both buyer and seller are jointly responsible for it, and county recorders collect it along with any local tax.

Local transfer tax is the part that varies. Municipalities and school districts may add their own share, and Pike County deeds can cross municipal lines, which is why the recorder asks for the local split in dollars. Ask the recorder or your closing agent for the combined rate that applies to your township or borough.

Some transfers pay nothing. The Department of Revenue lists exemptions for certain family transfers, transfers to governmental units and property passed by will or intestate succession. An heir who deeds an inherited Pike County house to a buyer is selling, so the later sale deed is taxed, but the original passing of title to the heir is not.

sections.h2: Where is Pike County and what is its housing like?
sections.html:
Pike County sits in the northeast corner of Pennsylvania along the Delaware River. It is the only Pennsylvania county that borders both New York and New Jersey. The county was organized in 1814 and named for General Zebulon Pike, and Milford is the seat. Matamoras is the largest borough, and the four largest settlements in the 2020 count are census-designated lake communities: Saw Creek, Hemlock Farms, Pocono Woodland Lakes and Pine Ridge.

The county covers 567 square miles, of which 545 are land. The terrain climbs from the river valley in the east to the foothills of the Poconos in the west, and the climate is humid continental. Interstate 84, US 6, US 209 and US 206 are among the major highways, and Census figures show a mean commute to work of 42.3 minutes.

  • Population estimate for July 1, 2025: 62,808, up 7.3 percent from the April 2020 base
  • Housing units, July 1, 2025: 40,861
  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 87.0 percent
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $272,600
  • Median household income, 2020 to 2024: $81,323
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $1,378

Those numbers come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for Pike County. With owners living in 87 percent of occupied homes, a typical Pike County sale is an owner selling to another buyer rather than a landlord exiting a rental.

sections.h2: How can I watch for fraud on my Pike County deed?
sections.html:
The recorder offers a fraud alert service through the county's online land records. You sign in at the Uslandrecords site, choose Pennsylvania and Pike County, register, and then use the Alerts menu to be told when a document is recorded under a name you choose. Setting up alerts does not need a credit card. Viewing or downloading images does.

This is worth doing before and after a sale. Before closing, an alert under your own name shows whether anything unexpected gets recorded against your property. After closing, it confirms that your sale deed reached the index. Copies of recorded deeds are available by contacting the office or through the Property Record Search.

sections.h2: What should an heir or a landlord with a Pike County house do before selling?
sections.html:
Start with the title. If the owner has died, the estate has to show who holds authority to sign, and that is a matter for the Register of Wills and your attorney. The Recorder of Deeds only records what is presented.

Next, check for open mortgages. A mortgage that was paid off years ago may still look open in the index until its satisfaction is recorded, and the recorder's office files satisfactions as part of its normal work. Your title company will want that cleared before closing.

Finally, think about timing. Tax bills, rent and repairs keep running while a deed waits for signatures. A seller who wants a fast, as-is closing can ask a buyer to accept the house without repairs, and the recording of the deed still follows the same steps described above.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Pike County?
faqs.a: At the Pike County Recorder of Deeds, 506 Broad Street in Milford, or through an electronic vendor. The county lists Simplifile and CSC for online recording. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 4:30.

faqs.q: What is the return fee on a rejected deed?
faqs.a: $10. The Pike County recorder charges that service fee on every returned document, so checking the acknowledgment and the amounts before you submit saves money and time.

faqs.q: Who pays realty transfer tax when a house sells?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller are jointly liable under the Department of Revenue's rules, although the purchase contract usually says who actually pays. The state rate is 1 percent, and local taxes can add to it. Ask the recorder or your closing agent for the local amount.

faqs.q: Is an inherited house exempt from transfer tax?
faqs.a: The passing of title by will or intestate succession is exempt under the Department of Revenue's list. A later sale of that house to a buyer is a separate transfer and is taxed like any other, unless a specific exemption applies.

faqs.q: Can I get a copy of my recorded deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Contact the Recorder of Deeds at 570-296-3508 or use the Property Record Search on the county's land records site. Viewing or downloading images through the online system requires registering a credit card.
